mainTopic: Which trees count as significant enough for the seller to keep back from a field sale (שיור), and what happens when a seller excludes one specific carob tree or sycamore trunk from the sale
overview: This amud opens by finishing a discussion about which trees a seller keeps for himself when he sells a field. The דייני גולה say that a tree the oxen's yoke can bend back is too minor to keep, and the גמרא explains that this fits with רב's rope test: רב's rule is for palm trees, and theirs is for other trees. Next, רב אחא בר הונא asks רב ששת about a seller who says 'except for this carob tree' or 'except for this sycamore trunk.' Do the other ones go to the buyer? רב ששת says no. He reads a ברייתא his way and proves his point with a field example: excluding a neighboring field does not sell all the seller's other fields. In a second version (איכא דאמרי), the question is about holding back half of one tree, and רב ששת rules that the buyer does not get even the other half. Finally, רב עמרם asks רב חסדא whether a שומר is believed to say 'I returned the deposit' while the owner still holds the שטר. רב חסדא says he is believed, because he has a מיגו: he could have claimed the items were taken by force. When רב עמרם pushes back, רב חסדא answers that the שטר would not help the owner against that claim either. רב עמרם's reply begins at the end of the amud and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The judges of the exile: the yoke test
steps.stepSummary: The דייני גולה rule that a tree the oxen's yoke can bend back is not kept by the seller, but a tree the yoke cannot bend back is kept.
steps.simpleTranslation: The judges of the exile say: any tree that the yoke of plowing oxen can bend back does not count as something the seller kept for himself. Any tree that the yoke cannot bend back does count as kept.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second opinion, from the דייני גולה, on which trees are important enough that a seller keeps them when he sells a field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before this, רב said that only trees you must climb with a rope count as kept by the seller. The דייני גולה give a different test. If the tree is so flexible that the oxen's yoke pushes it aside during plowing, it gets in nobody's way and is not significant. If it is sturdy enough to block the yoke, it is a real tree, and the seller keeps it.

keyTerms.meaning: The judges of the exile, the judges of Babylonia
Yoke, the wooden frame on plowing oxen
Presses it down or bends it back
Something the seller keeps back for himself from the sale

phrases.english: And the judges of the exile say:
Any tree that the yoke bends back,
phrases.notes: He means the yoke on oxen plowing under the tree.

phrases.english: is not something kept back by the seller.
Any tree that the yoke does not bend back
is something kept back by the seller.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second test, after רב's rope-climbing test from earlier in the סוגיא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A tree that the yoke can bend back is not kept by the seller. A tree that the yoke cannot bend back is kept by the seller.

steps.title: No real argument: palms versus other trees
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that רב and the דייני גולה do not argue. One test is for palm trees, and the other is for other trees.
steps.simpleTranslation: They do not really disagree. This rule (רב's) is about palm trees, and that rule (the judges of the exile) is about other trees.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles what looked like an argument by showing that each opinion is talking about a different kind of tree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Palm trees grow tall and straight, so the right test for them is whether you need a rope to climb them, as רב said. Other trees grow low and spread out, so the right test for them is the yoke test. Since each rule fits its own kind of tree, both rules are true at the same time.

keyTerms.meaning: And they do not disagree
Palm trees
Trees, meaning other kinds of trees

steps.whatToRemember: For palm trees, the seller keeps only the ones you must climb with a rope (רב). For other trees, he keeps only the ones the yoke cannot bend back (דייני גולה).

phrases.english: And they do not disagree:
this one is about palm trees, that one is about other trees.
phrases.notes: 'This one' is רב's rope test from before. 'That one' is the yoke test of the דייני גולה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Settles the apparent clash between step 1 and רב's earlier opinion.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each opinion covers a different kind of tree.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It looked like רב and the דייני גולה argue about which trees the seller keeps.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב's rule is for palm trees, and the yoke rule is for all other trees.

steps.title: Excluding one specific carob tree
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בר הונא asks רב ששת: if a seller excludes one particular carob or sycamore trunk, does the buyer get the other ones?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא בר הונא asked רב ששת: if a seller says 'except for this particular carob tree' or 'except for this particular sycamore trunk,' what is the law? Is it only that one carob that the buyer does not get, while he does get the other carobs? Or perhaps he does not get the other carobs either?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question begins. It is about a seller who names one special tree to leave out of the sale, and whether the other trees of that kind now go to the buyer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה taught that a grafted carob tree and a sycamore trunk are normally not included when a field is sold. So when the seller goes out of his way to exclude one of them, maybe he is hinting that the others are included. Or maybe he is just mentioning one, and the normal rule still holds for all of them.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked of him
Carob tree (here, a grafted one)
Trunk of a sycamore tree
Acquires
Or perhaps

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב אַחָא בַּר הוּנָא מֵרַב שֵׁשֶׁת:
phrases.english: Rav Acha bar Huna asked of Rav Sheshet:
If the seller said: "Except for such-and-such carob tree,"
or "Except for such-and-such sycamore trunk," what is the law?
Is it only that carob tree that the buyer does not acquire,
but the other carob trees he does acquire?

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא, שְׁאָר חָרוּבִין נָמֵי לָא קָנֵי?
phrases.english: Or perhaps he does not acquire the other carob trees either?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב אַחָא בַּר הוּנָא מֵרַב שֵׁשֶׁת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic connected to the משנה's rule about carobs and sycamore trunks.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does excluding one named carob or sycamore trunk mean that the other ones are included in the sale?

steps.title: רב ששת: the buyer does not get them
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת answers that the buyer does not acquire the other carob trees either.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: the buyer does not acquire them.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת gives a short answer. Naming one tree does not hand the other trees over to the buyer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The normal rule from the משנה stays in place: these trees are not part of the sale. Mentioning one specific tree does not change that for the rest.

keyTerms.meaning: He did not acquire

phrases.english: He said to him: He does not acquire them.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The buyer does not acquire the other carob trees or sycamore trunks.

steps.title: Challenge from a ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא challenges רב ששת from a ברייתא that seems to say only the named tree is not acquired.
steps.simpleTranslation: He raised an objection: a ברייתא says that if the seller said 'except for such-and-such carob tree' or 'except for such-and-such sycamore trunk,' the buyer does not acquire. Doesn't that mean only that one carob is not acquired, but the other carobs are acquired?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא quotes a ברייתא that he thinks goes against רב ששת's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says 'he does not acquire' about the named tree. רב אחא reads it as talking only about that one tree, which would suggest the other trees do go to the buyer. That would contradict רב ששת.

keyTerms.meaning: He raised an objection to him from an earlier source
What, is it not that...
The rest, the others

phrases.english: He raised an objection to him:
"Except for such-and-such carob tree," "except for such-and-such sycamore trunk,"
he does not acquire!

phrases.aramaic: מַאי, לָאו אוֹתוֹ חָרוּב הוּא דְּלֹא קָנָה,
phrases.english: What, is it not that only that carob tree is what he does not acquire,
but the other carob trees he does acquire?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב שישת's answer in step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's ruling that the buyer does not acquire the other carob trees.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא's 'he does not acquire' seems to apply only to the named tree, which implies the others are acquired.

steps.title: Reading the ברייתא differently
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת explains that the ברייתא means the buyer does not acquire even the other carob trees.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: No. It means he does not acquire even the other carob trees.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת answers the challenge by reading the ברייתא's words 'he does not acquire' as covering all the carob trees.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא never actually says what the buyer does not acquire. רב אחא assumed it meant only the named tree. רב ששת reads it as 'he does not acquire the others either,' which matches his own ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: Even
Also, either

steps.confusionAlert: Both sides agree that the named tree stays with the seller. The only argument is about the OTHER carob trees in the field.

phrases.english: He said to him: No.

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ שְׁאָר חָרוּבִין נָמֵי לֹא קָנָה.
phrases.english: He does not acquire even the other carob trees.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לָא; אֲפִילּוּ שְׁאָר חָרוּבִין נָמֵי לֹא קָנָה
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the source: the ברייתא's 'he does not acquire' covers the other trees too.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא means only the named tree is not acquired.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא means even the other carob trees are not acquired.

steps.title: Proof from excluding a neighboring field
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת proves his reading: if someone sells 'my field except for that other field,' nobody would say all his other fields are sold.
steps.simpleTranslation: Know that this is so: if a seller said, 'My field is sold to you except for such-and-such field,' would you say that only that field is not acquired, but all his other fields are acquired?! Rather, the buyer does not acquire them. Here too, he does not acquire the other carob trees.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת backs up his answer with a clear comparison that everyone would agree with.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Excluding a neighboring field obviously does not mean the seller is giving away every other field he owns. He only sold one field, and he just added a side remark. In the same way, naming one carob tree to leave out does not hand over the other carobs, which were never part of the sale to begin with.

keyTerms.meaning: Know (that it is so), introducing a proof
For if
Sold
The other ones
Here too

steps.whatToRemember: When a seller excludes one item that would not have been sold anyway, he is not hinting that the other items like it are included. They stay with the seller, just as the משנה says.
steps.whyThisMatters: This teaches a general rule for reading sale contracts: a side mention of one item does not change the default rule for everything else.

phrases.english: Know that this is so: for if he said to him:
"My field is sold to you
except for such-and-such field,"
would it be only that field that he does not acquire,
but the other fields he does acquire?!
Rather, he does not acquire them.
Here too, he does not acquire them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the reading given in step 6.
steps.raayaObject: רב ששת's ruling that the other carob trees are not acquired.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A comparison everyone accepts: excluding a neighboring field does not mean all of the seller's other fields are sold.

steps.title: Second version: what about holding back half of one tree?
steps.stepSummary: In the איכא דאמרי version, רב אחא בר הונא asks רב ששת about a seller who holds back half of a carob tree or half of a sycamore trunk. Does the buyer get the other half of that tree?
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say the question went like this: רב אחא בר הונא asked רב ששת about a seller who says 'except for half of this carob tree' or 'except for half of this sycamore trunk.' The buyer surely does not get the other carob trees. But does he get the half of this tree that the seller did not hold back? Or does he not get even that?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of the earlier question. This time the seller holds back only half of one tree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, everyone already agrees that the buyer does not get the other carob trees. The only open question is the leftover half of the named tree. Maybe the buyer gets it, because only half was held back. Or maybe the seller's words show he never meant to sell any part of that tree.

keyTerms.meaning: There are those who say: introduces a second version of a discussion
Half
The trunk of a sycamore tree
What he left over, meaning the part of the tree not held back
Or perhaps: introduces the other side of a question

steps.confusionAlert: This is not the same question as step 3. There, the seller held back a whole tree. Here, he holds back only half of one tree, and the other carob trees are already assumed not to be sold.

phrases.english: And there are those who say:

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב אַחָא בַּר הוּנָא מֵרַב שֵׁשֶׁת:
phrases.english: Rav Acha bar Huna asked Rav Sheshet:
"Except for half of such-and-such carob tree,"
"Except for half of such-and-such sycamore trunk": what is the law?
The other carob trees he certainly does not acquire,

phrases.aramaic: הָא מַה שֶּׁשִּׁיֵּיר בְּאוֹתוֹ חָרוּב – קָנֵי;
phrases.english: but what is left of that carob tree, he does acquire;
or perhaps,

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ מַה שֶּׁשִּׁיֵּיר בְּאוֹתוֹ חָרוּב נָמֵי לָא קָנֵי?
phrases.english: even what is left of that carob tree he also does not acquire?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב אַחָא בַּר הוּנָא מֵרַב שֵׁשֶׁת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Restarts the discussion of steps 3-7 in a second version, with a different case: half of one tree instead of a whole tree.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: When a seller holds back half of a named tree, does the buyer get the other half of that tree?

steps.title: רב ששת: the buyer does not get the rest of the tree
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת rules that the buyer does not get even the leftover half of that tree.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: He does not acquire it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת answers the question. The buyer gets no part of that tree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ששת picks the stricter side of the question. When the seller singled out this tree, it showed he was keeping the whole tree out of the sale. Saying 'half' does not turn the other half into part of the sale.

keyTerms.meaning: He said to him
Acquires, gets ownership
A carob tree

phrases.english: He said to him: He does not acquire.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The buyer does not get even the remaining half of the named tree.

steps.title: A ברייתא seems to say only the other trees are excluded
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא challenges רב ששת from a ברייתא. It says that in this case the buyer does not get 'the other carob trees.' That seems to imply he does get the leftover half of the named tree.
steps.simpleTranslation: He challenged him from a ברייתא: 'Except for half of this carob tree' or 'except for half of this sycamore trunk' means the buyer does not get the other carob trees. Doesn't that mean only the other trees are not his, but the rest of that tree is?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא brings a ברייתא that seems to go against רב ששת's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא lists only 'the other carob trees' as not sold. רב אחא reads that list as complete. If the leftover half of the named tree were also not sold, the ברייתא should have said so.

keyTerms.meaning: He challenged him from a ברייתא or משנה
What, is it not...? Introduces a suggested reading that creates the challenge
The other carob trees

phrases.english: He raised an objection to him:
"Except for half of such-and-such carob tree,"
"except for half of such-and-such sycamore trunk":
he did not acquire the other carob trees.

phrases.aramaic: מַאי, לָאו שְׁאָר חָרוּבִין הוּא דְּלָא קָנָה,
phrases.english: What, is it not that it is the other carob trees that he did not acquire,

phrases.aramaic: הָא מַה שֶּׁשִּׁיֵּיר בְּאוֹתוֹ חָרוּב – קָנָה?
phrases.english: but what is left of that carob tree, he did acquire?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the ruling of step 9 using a ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's ruling that the buyer does not get the leftover half of the tree.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא names only the other trees as not sold, which implies the rest of the named tree is sold.

steps.title: The ברייתא means even the rest of that tree is not sold
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת rejects רב אחא's reading. The ברייתא means the buyer does not get even the leftover half of that tree.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: No. He does not get even what is left of that carob tree.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת defends his ruling by reading the ברייתא differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אחא assumed the ברייתא was naming the only thing the buyer does not get. רב ששת says it is not a complete list. Besides the other carob trees, the buyer also does not get the leftover half of the named tree.

keyTerms.meaning: No: rejects the suggested reading
Even
Also, too

phrases.english: He said to him: No;

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ מַה שֶּׁשִּׁיֵּיר בְּאוֹתוֹ חָרוּב נָמֵי לֹא קָנָה.
phrases.english: even what is left of that carob tree he also did not acquire.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the ברייתא: it does not give a complete list of what is not sold.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא lists everything the buyer does not get, so the rest of the named tree is sold.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rest of the named tree is not sold either. The ברייתא's wording does not imply otherwise.

steps.title: Proof from holding back half of another field
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת proves his reading. Suppose a seller says, 'my field is sold to you except for half of that other field.' Nobody would say the buyer gets the other half of that other field. So here too, the buyer does not get the rest of the tree.
steps.simpleTranslation: Know that this is true. If someone said, 'My field is sold to you except for half of that field,' would you say only that half is not sold but the other half is? Of course not. The buyer gets none of it. Here too, he gets none of the tree.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת backs up his answer with a comparison that everyone would agree with.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The seller described the sale as 'my field.' The other field was never part of it. Mentioning 'half' of the other field does not quietly add its second half to the sale. The same is true of the named tree: the seller's mention of half of it does not sell the other half.

keyTerms.meaning: Know (that this is so): introduces a supporting proof
The other one, the remaining part
Here too: applies the proof to our case

steps.whatToRemember: In both versions, רב ששת holds the same idea. When a seller singles out a tree as held back, the buyer gets no part of that tree, even if the seller said only 'half.'

phrases.english: Know that this is so,
for if he had said to him:
"My field is sold to you
except for half of such-and-such field":
phrases.notes: This is a separate field next to the one being sold, so it was never part of the sale.

phrases.aramaic: הָהוּא הוּא דְּלָא קָנָה, הָא אִידַּךְ קָנָה?!
phrases.english: is it only that half that he did not acquire, but the other half he did acquire?!
Rather, he does not acquire it;
here too, he does not acquire it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the reading of the ברייתא given in step 11.
steps.raayaObject: רב ששת's reading that the leftover half of the named tree is not sold.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A logical comparison: holding back half of a separate field obviously does not sell its other half.

steps.title: Is a שומר believed to say 'I returned it' when the owner holds the שטר?
steps.stepSummary: רב עמרם asks רב חסדא about someone who gave a פקדון to a שומר with a signed שטר. The שומר now says, 'I returned it.' Is he believed because of a מיגו? Or does the owner's holding of the שטר show that the item was never returned?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב עמרם asked רב חסדא: Someone deposited items with his friend and got a signed document recording it. Later the friend says, 'I gave them back to you.' What is the law? Do we say that since he could have claimed 'they were taken by force' and been believed, he is believed now too? Or can the owner say, 'If you gave them back, why is the document against you still in my hand?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic. It is a question about how believable a שומר is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One side uses a מיגו: the שומר could have claimed an אונס and been believed, so he should be believed when he makes this claim instead. The other side points to the שטר still in the owner's hand. Someone who returns a deposit would normally take back the document, so the owner's holding it suggests the items were not returned.

keyTerms.meaning: One who deposits an item with someone else to look after
A signed document, here a record of the deposit
Since: he is believed because he could have made a stronger claim
They were taken by force, lost through something he could not prevent
Do we say...? Introduces the first side of a question

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב עַמְרָם מֵרַב חִסְדָּא:
phrases.english: Rav Amram asked Rav Chisda:
One who deposits items with his fellow with a document,
and the other says to him: "I returned them to you": what is the law?
phrases.notes: The speaker here is the שומר, the one who was holding the items.

phrases.english: Do we say:
since, if he wanted, he could have said "they were taken by force" and he would be believed,
now too he is believed;
or perhaps the owner can say to him:
"What is your document doing in my hand?"
phrases.notes: He means: if you really returned the items, you would have taken back the document that records the deposit against you.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב עַמְרָם מֵרַב חִסְדָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic, unrelated to the carob tree discussion.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the owner's holding of the שטר outweigh the שומר's מיגו when the שומר claims he returned the deposit?

steps.title: רב חסדא: the שומר is believed
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא rules that the שומר is believed when he says he returned the items.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: He is believed.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא answers רב עמרם's question. The שומר's word is accepted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא goes with the מיגו side. Since the שומר could have claimed an אונס and been believed, the owner's holding of the שטר does not take away his credibility when he says he returned the items.

keyTerms.meaning: He is believed
I returned them
Your document is in my hand: the owner's argument, which רב חסדא does not accept here

steps.whatToRemember: According to רב חסדא, a שומר who says 'I returned it' is believed, even though the owner still holds the שטר, because of the מיגו that he could have claimed an אונס.

phrases.english: He said to him: He is believed.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The שומר is believed that he returned the items, based on the מיגו.

steps.title: Why is the document still with the owner?
steps.stepSummary: רב עמרם challenges רב חסדא's ruling. The owner should be able to say: 'If you returned my items, why is your שטר still in my hand?'
steps.simpleTranslation: But let the owner say to him: 'What is your document doing in my hand?'
steps.whatsHappening: רב עמרם attacks רב חסדא's ruling that the שומר is believed. He argues that the owner still holding the שטר should prove the items were never returned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, when a שומר returns a פקדון, he takes back the שטר he wrote. The owner still has it, so it looks like nothing was returned. רב עמרם is saying the שטר should beat the שומר's claim and his מיגו.

keyTerms.meaning: A signed document. Here, the one the שומר wrote to confirm he received the פקדון.
What is it doing (here)? Literally, 'what does it want?'
An item left with someone for safekeeping.
The person watching someone else's item.

phrases.english: But let him say to him:
phrases.notes: The owner of the items is speaking to the שומר.

phrases.english: 'What is your document doing in my hand?!'
phrases.notes: 'Your document' means the שטר that records the deposit against the שומר. If he really returned the items, he would have taken it back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב חסדא's ruling in step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב חסדא's ruling that the שומר is believed when he says 'I returned it.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The owner still holds the שטר. That should prove the items were never returned and outweigh the שומר's מיגו.

steps.title: The same document would not help against 'they were taken by force'
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא answers with a comparison. If the שומר had claimed נאנסו, the owner could not use the שטר against him. So the שטר cannot disprove 'I returned it' either.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: By your reasoning, if the שומר had said 'they were taken by force,' could the owner say, 'What is your document doing in my hand?'
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא defends his ruling. He shows that the owner's 'why do I still have the שטר' argument fails in a parallel case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the items were lost by אונס, the שטר would naturally still be with the owner, so it proves nothing there. The שומר could have used that claim, so he has a מיגו. The שטר therefore does not undercut his claim that he returned the items.

keyTerms.meaning: And according to your reasoning. It turns the other side's logic back on him.
They were taken or lost through forces beyond his control (אוֹנֶס).
Is able to, can.
Since he could have made a better claim, he is believed on the claim he made.

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a document proving a deposit was made does not, by itself, prove the deposit is still owed.

phrases.english: He said to him: And according to your reasoning,
phrases.notes: רב חסדא is answering רב עמרם.

phrases.english: if he had said to him, 'They were taken by force,'
would he be able to say to him:
'What is your document doing in my hand?!'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב עמרם's challenge in step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Parallel case (וְלִיטַעְמָיךְ). The challenger's argument would also fail in a case he must agree with.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The owner holding the שטר proves the items were never returned.
steps.terutzMaskana: The שטר also stays with the owner when the items are lost by אונס. So it proves nothing against the שומר, and his מיגו stands.

steps.title: רב עמרם begins his reply
steps.stepSummary: רב עמרם starts to answer רב חסדא's comparison. His actual words continue in the next part of the גמרא.
steps.whatsHappening: This line is only a setup. רב עמרם is about to respond to רב חסדא's comparison, and his response comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only the opening words of the reply appear here. רב עמרם will try to show why the נאנסו case is different from the 'I returned it' case.

keyTerms.meaning: The אמורא who asked the question and is pushing back here.
The אמורא who ruled that the שומר is believed.

phrases.english: He said to him:
phrases.notes: Now רב עמרם is speaking again. His point continues in the next lines.
